sources.title: Reports of violence against women in Gaza surge, UN agency finds
sources.excerpt: The UN Population Fund also says there has been a "severe escalation" in the number of early and forced marriages.
sources.text: Reports of violence against women in Gaza surge, UN agency finds. It also warns that there has been a "severe escalation" in the number of early and forced marriage incidents in the second quarter of this year. Both are considered types of gender-based violence (GBV) by the UN. Another report presenting testimony from 230 women in crowded displacement camps in Gaza City and Khan Younis , external makes for a grim read, describing the violence they have experienced or witnessed. One displaced woman in a school-turned-shelter in Gaza highlights how rape victims are often married to their rapists to avoid shame and scandal. "When rape cases are discovered in schools, you find weddings and celebrations at the school the next day," she says. Another woman tells how last year, at the time of famine, "a man married off his 14-year-old daughter in exchange for two bags of flour so he and his [other] children could eat". Six women in different displacement camps shared stories of such exchanges - which would have been unthinkable before the conflict between Israel and Hamas began in 2023. Although data collection to establish actual figures remains tricky, in the second quarter of this year, the UNFPA says the number of reported cases of early and forced marriage had increased by 123% on the first quarter. Early or child marriage involved girls aged 12 to 17. "The trends are shocking," says Nestor Owomuhangi, the UNFPA representative to Palestine. He says that the extreme circumstances over the past three years - which have seen tens of thousands of people killed, mass destruction and multiple waves of displacement in Gaza - have broken down social structures, so "everything is eroded... there is no system". While food markets have reopened, many cannot afford the goods on offer, there is still extreme poverty and hunger with reliance on charitable handouts. Nearly all the population of more than two million Gazans have been driven from their homes, leaving most living in squalid tent camps or damaged buildings. Public services have largely collapsed, and Israeli air strikes have continued despite the ceasefire. Prior to the war, girls in Gaza outnumbered and outperformed boys at every level of education above primary school. Now, with prolonged school closures, many children have dropped out of education. For boys there is pressure to find informal work to help support their families, for girls there are heightened issues around safety. Living among strangers, without privacy, in a socially conservative society, there are complaints of heightened sexual harassment and abuse - many families see marrying their daughters as a way to protect them and preserve modesty. The UNFPA report - based on research carried out in late 2025 and early 2026 - reveals how girls orphaned during the war are especially vulnerable. One woman in a Gaza City camp interviewed for the report says she attended the wedding of two girls from her family, aged just 14 and 15. "Their uncles married them off very young. Do you know why? Because their father and mother were martyred, and their uncles wanted to get rid of the responsibility and expenses," the woman said. "By God, they don't understand what marriage or life is." The Women's Affairs Center in Gaza - a Palestinian NGO which works with the UNFPA - and other support groups have documented distressing cases of girls who have been married and suffered abuse, often becoming pregnant. They say that those in their early teens are much more likely to have miscarriages and underweight babies than adult women. "We see adolescent pregnancies going through the roof because of child marriage," says Owomuhangi. "A child who is at an age when the body is not fully developed to sustain another body, who is hungry, in unhygienic circumstances, who doesn't know how to take care of the infant, who doesn't even know how to take care of herself, the consequences of that pregnancy are always really, really bad." The UN and most humanitarian organisations categorise marriages of girls under 18 as early marriage. Even before the war, this was more common among Palestinians in Hamas-run Gaza than it was in the occupied West Bank, but it was declining. The law in Gaza allows exceptions to the minimum marital age of 17 with parental consent and authorisation by a judge. Court officials can approve marriage for those as young as 14 years and seven months old, although a local Sharia expert told us that "legal safeguards" had been removed when Islamic courts - which officiate over family matters for Muslims - were closed for a large part of the war. The BBC has been speaking to some families in which bereaved relatives were married. Zuhair, who is 25, says his uncles pushed him to marry a 16-year-old girl from his extended family after her father - her sole guardian - was killed in an Israeli air strike. Challenged on why he agreed to go ahead with the plan, he said: "One of the reasons that led me to marry her was that there was no one to take care of her. That's the first point." "If it were not for the war, she would still be a young girl spoiled by her father. She would be going to school," Zuhair adds. "She still has a child's mindset, not a mature mindset. She misses school, her family, friends. She even misses simply sitting at home." A couple says they allowed their 17-year-old son to marry his 16-year-old cousin after their older son and the girl's father were killed. The teenager is now pregnant so will not return to school. "She needs to care for her child," her father-in-law says, "her education would be in vain." Sexual violence in Gaza remains acutely under-reported in large part due to fear of stigma and retaliation. UN safety audits have shown particular risks to women and girls at night, causing them to avoid camp toilets and bathrooms. The latest analysis report by the UNFPA-led task force stated that incidents of sexual violence, including rape and sexual assault, "have become critical in Gaza". They accounted for 2.7% of total reported

sources.title: Israel strikes Gaza on October 7 anniversary, three dead: officials
sources.excerpt: Loud bangs across the border in Gaza were audible from the site of the Nova music festival just as family members gathered at dawn to mourn the more than 300 revellers killed three years earlier
sources.text: Israel strikes Gaza on October 7 anniversary, three dead: officials. Loud bangs across the border in Gaza were audible from the site of the Nova music festival just as family members gathered at dawn to mourn the more than 300 revellers killed three years earlier. In Gaza City, Al-Shifa hospital reported two people killed in an Israeli strike overnight. Gaza's civil defence identified one of the dead as Mohamed Tamous and said he was a volunteer for the agency, which serves as an emergency rescue service under Hamas. The Israeli military said it struck and killed "two Hamas terrorists who had exited Kamal Adwan Hospital in the northern Gaza Strip," adding that one had "planted explosives... in the area of the Yellow Line with the intention of harming IDF troops." The so-called Yellow Line demarcates the areas under Hamas and Israeli military control in the Gaza Strip. The military identified one of those killed in the strike as Tamous, whom it said was a sniper in Hamas's military wing while simultaneously working for the civil defence. In the southern city of Khan Yunis, Nasser Hospital said that a 60-year-old man, Hisham Ibrahim Abu Mustafa, was killed in an Israeli strike and that others were injured. On the third anniversary of the first day of the war in Gaza, living conditions remain dire in the coastal Palestinian territory, despite a U.S.-brokered ceasefire that came into effect in October 2025. "After three years of siege, killing and destruction, Israel has turned the Gaza Strip into an uninhabitable place," said Gaza City resident Mahmoud Abu Hasira. Hundreds of thousands of displaced people still live in tent cities and makeshift shelters that sprawl on beaches or next to piles of rubble from bombed-out residential buildings. "We once had homes, but now we have lost our loved ones, whose bodies still lie beneath the rubble," said Bassam Nasser, a resident of Beit Hanoun, a now largely destroyed city in Gaza's north, who was displaced in the early days of the war. Israel says it controls about 60% of Gaza, on the territory's outer perimeter, including Beit Hanoun, while most of the Palestinian population lives in the remaining Hamas-controlled areas. Though Israel eased its restrictions on aid trucks entering Gaza after the ceasefire, Ahmed Nasser, another resident of Gaza City, told AFP that life remained desperately hard. "The war and the famine have left us hungry, fearful and displaced, living in tents and struggling with soaring prices," he said. Israel's military offensive has displaced nearly the entire population of Gaza and killed more than 74,200 people, according to Gaza's health ministry, which is under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations. sources.title: Israelis mourn October 7 attack as Palestinians in Gaza live in ruins of war
sources.excerpt: Israelis are gathering Wednesday to commemorate the third anniversary of the October 7 attack that killed 1,200 people and saw 251 taken hostage. In Gaza, the territory's almost two million people live in ruins.
sources.text: Israelis mourn October 7 attack as Palestinians in Gaza live in ruins of war. Israelis gathered Wednesday to commemorate the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack that killed 1,200 people, saw 251 taken hostage and sparked a devastating war in Gaza that has left much of the territory in ruins. In southern Israel, families mourned at intersections, bomb shelters and the site of a music festival that the militants overran three years ago in the deadliest attack in the country's history. It is the first anniversary since all the hostages, living and dead, were returned, marking a new stage of grief. For Palestinians, the anniversary brings another day of misery after as Israel's war in Gaza killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. Several international NGOs as well as a UN commission have found that Israel has committed genocide in the Gaza Strip. Most Gaza residents live in vast, squalid tent camps, with large parts of the strip’s cities reduced to rubble. More than half the territory remains in the hands of the Israeli military. Despite a ceasefire deal reached nearly a year ago, Israeli strikes continue almost daily. For the region, the day highlights a startling transformation over the past three years. Israeli troops occupy a large chunk of southern Lebanon in their conflict with the Hezbollah militant group, which began firing on Israel in 2023 in support of Hamas. Iran and the United States are locked in a confrontation that has seen attacks across Gulf Arab countries and has shaken the global economy — a conflict that Israel helped launch and that the Gaza war paved the way for, even if they weren’t directly connected. Near the town of Reim, where the music festival was underway when militants attacked, families gathered around photos of their killed relatives. Hundreds of people paid their respects to the more than 350 people killed in and around the festival site. Videos from that day showed militants gunning down fleeing revelers, shooting the wounded at point-blank range and ambushing those seeking refuge in nearby bomb shelters. On Wednesday, survivors' relatives hugged at 6:29 a.m. — the exact time the first rockets were launched three years ago — as explosions boomed in nearby Gaza. Anya Davitashili, who lost her 25-year-old son, Sean, said she visits the site every Saturday. It’s where she feels closest to him. “I have a video of him dancing here that ends at 6:29 in the morning, it’s in front of my eyes all the time,” she said. “Every morning, you wake up and there is just endless missing.” Elkana Bohbot, 37, is marking the anniversary in Israel for the first time since his release after 738 days of captivity. For most of that time, he said, he was held underground in a dark, damp tunnel. Bohbot, who was abducted from the festival, was kept in a small cell with other hostages, given little food and allowed to bathe only every few weeks, he said. His captors forced him to take part in propaganda videos, including one where he acts out a fake call to his family. In the year since his release, Bohbot has undergone physical and emotional rehabilitation. In August, his wife, Rivka, gave birth to a daughter, fulfilling his promise to himself in the tunnels to give his 5-year-old son, Reem, a sibling. The newborn Michele is “ not a symbol for my people, she is more of a symbol for the enemy,” Bohbot told The Associated Press. “This child is the message for you that we were here and we will always be here forever.” No events are expected Wednesday in Gaza, but Hamas in a statement praised the October 7 attack as an example of “heroism, resilience and national solidarity” and said it had returned the Palestinian cause to the world’s attention. “The conflict with the enemy did not begin on that day, as its final chapters are not written yet,” it said. Palestinians in the territory said the extent to which their lives had deteriorated over the past three years was previously unimaginable. “We witnessed death, destruction, and bombardment that we had never known before,” said Walid Akram, a Gaza City resident who, like most in Gaza, has been displaced by the war. Raed Khozeiq’s coastal neighborhood in Tel al-Hawa was largely flattened. Nothing about his life now is the same, he said. “No country in the world has gone through what we have experienced here,” he said. “A war of extermination, starvation, the absence of schools and universities — nothing remains.” More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's Health Ministry. Since the ceasefire that took effet on October 10, 2025, Israeli strikes have killed 1,460 Palestinians in Gaza, according to the ministry. Seven Israeli soldiers have been killed in that period. Restrictions on the entry of goods and aid have contributed to a hunger crisis, food security experts say.

sources.title: Israelis mark three years since Hamas attack that set off Gaza assault
sources.excerpt: The anniversary is the first for Israelis without any hostages still held in Gaza, ⁠with those dead and alive exchanged in swaps with Hamas for Palestinians held in Israeli jails. The remains of the last Israeli hostage were recovered in January
sources.text: Israelis mark three years since Hamas attack that set off Gaza assault. The anniversary is the first for Israelis without any hostages still held in Gaza, ⁠with those dead and alive exchanged in swaps with Hamas for Palestinians held in Israeli jails. The remains of the last Israeli hostage were recovered in January. It also comes just 20 days ahead of Israel’s first election since the attack, a vote ​that is viewed as a referendum ‌on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s long tenure in power. Mr. Netanyahu has rejected blame for the security breach and resisted calls for an independent investigation. That has frustrated many in Israel, including families of those killed in the attacks, some of whom have joined the election race. A poll by the Israel Democracy ‌Institute showed that 68% of Jewish Israelis said that the events of October 7 were ​a very central or fairly central element in their decision of which party to vote for. Election polls show neither Mr. Netanyahu nor his main competitors would muster enough seats in ⁠parliament to form a coalition if a vote were held today. The anniversary is also the first since an October 10, 2025, U.S.-brokered ceasefire deal that halted major fighting ‌but has failed to stop Israeli attacks in Gaza or secure the disarmament of Hamas and other militant groups. The deal left Israel in control of some 53% of Gaza, since expanded by Israeli forces to nearly two-thirds. Hamas controls the remaining third, where the 2 million population mostly live in makeshift tents and bombed out buildings. US President Donald Trump’s so-called “Board of Peace” has proposed several plans that would see Gaza rebuilt. But those plans, which fail to account for the property rights of Palestinians whose homes were destroyed, ‌have failed to gain the buy-in of Israel or Hamas, which are still deadlocked in ceasefire talks. The two have yet to ​agree on the terms of a deal that would see Hamas lay down its weapons in exchange for Israeli troop withdrawals. Israel says it will not pull back ⁠until Hamas fully disarms; Hamas says it has agreed to a phased process but will not disarm so long ⁠as Israeli attacks continue. Israel has kept up a bombing campaign in Gaza that has killed a number of Hamas militants in recent months but has also killed many civilians, say ‌Gaza health authorities, whose death figures do not distinguish between civilians and combatants. More than 1,400 Palestinians in Gaza have been killed since the October 2025 ceasefire, the health authorities say. During the same ​time, five Israeli soldiers have been killed by militants or in combat, the military says. Comments have to be in English, and in full sentences. They cannot be abusive or personal. sources.title: One Year Into Gaza's So-Called Ceasefire, Palestinians Still Live Among Devastation
sources.excerpt: Palestinians in Gaza continue to deal with Israeli airstrikes, limited food and water, mass displacement and a humanitarian aid shortage.
sources.text: One Year Into Gaza's So-Called Ceasefire, Palestinians Still Live Among Devastation. Almost exactly one year after Israel reached a fragile ceasefire agreement with Hamas, Palestinians in Gaza continue to deal with the lingering effects of what human rights groups , United Nations experts and relevant scholars have all concluded is genocide — including Israeli airstrikes, limited food and water, mass displacement and a severe humanitarian aid shortage. Israel currently controls about 70% of the strip, setting what’s been dubbed a “yellow line” that bars Palestinians from crossing. Since the ceasefire on Oct. 10, 2025, the Gaza Health Ministry has recorded more than 1,400 Palestinians killed and 4,880 injured. Part of Israel’s control includes limiting access to humanitarian aid. According to the U.N., approved aid can only be brought into the strip via one crossing at the southern tip of the enclave. Humanitarian officials have been begging for Israel to allow more than the current sliver of aid to enter so that food, medical, hygiene and shelter needs can be met. “A truck full of non-priority supplies or the right supplies arriving too late, doesn’t save lives. That’s the question that actually matters,” Dr. Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, the World Health Organization representative for Palestine, said last week. Palestinian face increased dangers because of housing instability after Israel essentially flattened the territory over the past three years. As of Sept. 20, the U.N. says that 94% of Gaza’s population remains in urgent need of shelter and basic household assistance. Israel has not allowed construction supplies in to help rebuild the homes, schools, hospitals and mosques reduced to rubble. “As winter begins, this urgency to get supplies into Gaza only deepens,” Van De Weerdt said, warning of preventable disease outbreaks and rodents. “Almost two million people are in need of shelter to protect against the cold and the risk of flooding, exposing people to serious health and safety risks, let alone [their] dignity.” In addition to shelter supplies, Israel is severely limiting the amount of food and supplies for meal production, fueling the ongoing hunger crisis facing Palestinians — particularly children, who require more sustenance for growth and disease prevention. U.N. personnel have previously described Israel blocking humanitarians from bringing in peanut butter as nutritional assistance for children, claiming it’s a “luxury” and that Hamas may steal it. “It is insane, because on the other hand, they are allowing chocolates and they are allowing sugar into Gaza, but they do not allow something like peanut butter, which is nutritious,” Jaser AbuMousa, a Middle East Institute fellow from Gaza, told The New Yorker last month . “The U.N. was hoping that it would be helpful because of all the malnutrition that the people are suffering from. So their claim that it’s a luxury is nonsense.” The lack of shelter and nutritious food has kept Palestinians susceptible to disease, made worse by a collapsed sewage network and a struggling hospital system with few medical supplies coming in. “Most people have less than 1.5 gallons of water per day and limited access to basic hygiene items such as soap and detergent,” Dr. Murad Asaliyya, Gaza medical activities manager for Doctors Without Borders, said in a statement. “We are treating gastroenteritis, acute respiratory infections, a lot of skin conditions, hepatitis, bacterial skin infections, scabies and lice,” Asaliyya continued. “At the same time, we are facing severe shortages in terms of medical supplies. Even the cream we need to treat scabies has been restricted by the Israeli authorities.” Progress on the ceasefire agreement has been at a standstill as Israel continues attacking Gaza while severely limiting aid. The so-called Board of Peace created by the Trump administration has been given authority to oversee Gaza’s rebuilding , but the board’s representative recently argued that Israel’s ongoing strikes threaten the deal as well as any chance of Hamas disarming. Speaking to The New Yorker, AbuMousa said that the lack of progress means daily life for Gazans has felt like a tense waiting game. “The tone is completely desperate, to be honest. I mean, the waiting without anything moving is making people angry, and they cannot respond positively,” he said. “I mean, they cannot engage in a normal conversation. I understand this. I totally understand this.”

sources.title: ‘Neither war nor peace’: Palestinians in Gaza on existing amid disease, despair and ruins
sources.excerpt: People tell of lives changed beyond recognition after the 7 October attacks by Hamas three years ago and the subsequent Israeli offensive Ahmed Ishtaiwi has six chairs. They are cheap and plastic and battered, but they are among the 43-year-old driver and mechanic’s most valuable possessions. Continue reading...
sources.text: ‘Neither war nor peace’: Palestinians in Gaza on existing amid disease, despair and ruins. Ahmed Ishtaiwi has six chairs. They are cheap and plastic and battered, but they are among the 43-year-old driver and mechanic’s most valuable possessions. Ishtaiwi lives in a tent near Deir al-Balah in central Gaza with his two daughters. Their former home is far to the north, in the now ruined town of Beit Lahiya, uninhabitable and impossible to reach. “When I sit on those chairs, I remember sitting in the garden at home, having breakfast and drinking tea. They remind me of my life there,” he said last week. Wednesday is the anniversary of the raid on 7 October 2023 by Hamas militants into southern Israel that killed 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and triggered a relentless Israeli military offensive that killed 73,000 Palestinians, mostly civilians, wounded many more and reduced swathes of Gaza to rubble. When Layan al-Jbour, a 15-year-old from the southern city of Khan Younis, tries to bring some order to the crowded makeshift shelter she shares with her parents, brothers and sisters in al-Mawasi, a strip of coastline at the southernmost end of Gaza, she recalls life before the war. “When I tidy the tent, I remember our home and how I used to tidy it. I remember my room and how I used to make my bed. When I put a sheet over a table and arrange the bedding, the place looks like our old home,” al-Jbour said. “We hardly took anything with us from our home. We left everything behind, and the only thing I took was my schoolbag. It is the most precious thing I own now. It reminds me so much of my school days. I loved going to school and meeting my friends there.” Across Gaza, Palestinians describe daily routines full of challenges that nothing in their former lives prepared them for: shortages of water and of nourishing food, minimal healthcare, disease, unemployment, economic collapse and the continuing threat of death or injury. Despite a ceasefire a year ago, Israel’s airstrikes continue. Palestinians who have approached the “yellow line” that divides Gaza into zones controlled by the Israeli military and by Hamas have been shot dead. In the last year, the overall death toll has risen by a further 1,400 people. In recent days, Israeli attacks have intensified, killing at least two Palestinians in Gaza on Tuesday, according to health officials. The Israeli military said the strikes targeted militants. On Wednesday, Gaza medics said at ​least two Palestinians were killed and others wounded in airstrikes in Beit Lahiya and Khan Younis. “It is what we feared … a ceasefire that just isn’t a ceasefire,” said one international aid worker now based in Amman, Jordan, who worked in Gaza throughout much of the conflict. “Daily life is horrible. People aren’t hungry any more but they are still malnourished. Our local staff are telling us that this is just the next stage of the conflict.” Ramiz Alakbarov, the UN’s humanitarian coordinator for the Occupied Palestinian Territory, told the UN security council last month that despite the increase in supplies entering Gaza, the health situation remained critical, with “infectious diseases … widespread amid overcrowded displacement sites and inadequate water, sanitation and hygiene conditions”. Inadequate funding for relief efforts exacerbated the “shortages of medical supplies, fuel and the overall humanitarian response”, Alakbarov said, while “restrictions on the entry of critical humanitarian items imposed by Israel” were slowing preparations for cold weather. Israeli authorities deny shortages and say adequate supplies are reaching Gaza, with more than 600 trucks entering the territory each day. Saleh Kilani, 70, from Beit Lahiya, used to have a farm and olive trees before the war. “Around this time of year, I used to press about 60 containers of olive oil. But I lost all of that too. If I go to my home I may die, and if I go to my farm, I may die too. This is not a life. We are exhausted and we have lost hope.” Kilani said life before the conflict seemed very distant. “We never used to think twice about seeing orange and peach trees, green fields, grapes and figs. These things were simply part of our lives. Now when we see them, we are surprised,” he said. Hamas, which swiftly reimposed its authority over the 2.3 million Palestinians who live in the third of Gaza not under the control of the Israeli military, has rebuilt a rudimentary administration which provides patchy education, some healthcare services and limited policing based on deterrence through often arbitrary punishment. Donald Trump’s plan to definitively end the war in Gaza has stalled, with little progress towards disarming Hamas, securing the withdrawal of Israeli troops and beginning the vast job of reconstruction. “My biggest fear is that this situation will continue. We are living through a period that can be described as neither war nor peace,” said Kilani. The only time Esraa Abu Taiba recalls her life before the war is when she gets to practise her former profession: beautician. The 26-year-old lived in Bani Suheila, a town to the east of Khan Younis and now within the zone controlled by Israel. Of her five brothers, two were killed in the conflict, two were wounded, and one is among the more than 1,500 Palestinians from Gaza in detention in Israel. “Before the war my life was quiet and good,” she said. “I could go wherever I wanted without fear or restrictions. We lived in our own home. We had a washing machine, a tap and a garden. The house belonged to us and we lived there comfortably. “Now we live in a tent. Our lives depend on carrying water and getting food from the community kitchen. A water truck comes to the end of the street and … I go to collect it because my mother cannot carry it.” Like most Palestinians in Gaza, her family was displaced multiple times during the conflict, and they have lost everything from their former home – except a house key, which her mother keeps close. “The only thing I still do from my old life is some beauty work. sources.title: Zohran Mamdani faces backlash for calling Israel’s Gaza war ‘ongoing genocide’ on Oct 7 anniversary
sources.text: Zohran Mamdani faces backlash for calling Israel’s Gaza war ‘ongoing genocide’ on Oct 7 anniversary. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Wednesday marked the third anniversary of the October 7 Hamas attack on Israel by condemning the killings and hostage-taking, while also accusing the Israeli government of carrying out an “ongoing genocide” in Gaza.Mamdani’s statement, issued as Israel and Jewish communities marked three years since the Hamas attack, acknowledged that Hamas killed more than 1,100 Israelis and abducted 251 people. He described the loss as “unthinkable” but said the suffering in the region “did not begin nor end” on October 7.The New York mayor also highlighted the Palestinian death toll in Gaza, saying more than 74,000 Palestinians, including more than 21,000 children, have been killed. He accused Israel of bombing ambulances, residential buildings and journalists and of restricting food aid from entering Gaza.Mamdani described the Israeli government’s military campaign as an “ongoing genocide” and also referred to alleged “war crimes”, “occupation” and “apartheid” in his statement.Nikki Haley attacks Mamdani over Oct 7 statementFormer US ambassador to the UN Nikki Haley sharply criticised Mamdani over his remarks. “Shame on you for trying to blow a kiss and slap Israelis in the face at the same time,” Haley said in a post on X.Haley accused Hamas of having “raped, burned, and murdered Israelis and Americans” on October 7 and said hostages were kidnapped and tortured for months.“This is antisemitism, no matter how you try to put a bow on it,” Haley said, adding that Israelis had the right to defend themselves.Israeli officials, Jewish groups criticise MamdaniMamdani’s comments also drew criticism from Israeli officials and Jewish organisations, who accused him of turning an anniversary meant to remember the victims of the October 7 attack into criticism of Israel.Israeli UN Ambassador Danny Danon told the New York Post that Mamdani was attempting to “hijack” a day dedicated to victims and survivors.Danon compared the move to using the anniversary of the September 11 attacks in the US to focus on criticism of America rather than the victims and the al-Qaeda attackers.The controversy comes days after Jewish organisations criticised aspects of Mamdani’s strategy to combat antisemitism in New York. The UJA-Federation of New York, JCRC-NY, AJC New York and the New York Board of Rabbis said the policy had positive elements but warned that rhetoric that “demonizes and delegitimizes Israel” could contribute to the targeting of Jewish New Yorkers.Mamdani, who has long criticised the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza, was scheduled to attend an October 7 remembrance vigil before meeting Palestinian New Yorkers, according to reports.You use AI every day. sources.excerpt: The Gaza peace plan, officially the Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict, is a multilateral agreement between Israel and Hamas that aims to address the ongoing Gaza war and broader Middle Eastern crisis. Led by United States president Donald Trump, it was negotiated in consultation with many Arab and Muslim…
sources.text: Gaza peace plan. The Gaza peace plan, officially the Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict, is a multilateral agreement between Israel and Hamas that aims to address the ongoing Gaza war and broader Middle Eastern crisis. Led by United States president Donald Trump, it was negotiated in consultation with many Arab and Muslim countries. The plan was announced by Trump on September 29, 2025, during a press conference at the White House alongside Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu. It was signed on October 9, coming into effect the following day, and was endorsed by the United Nations Security Council on November 17.
